title: JGB Yield Curve Steepness: 10-Year vs 30-Year Dynamics
abstract: A careful look at the long end of the JGB curve, where the BoJ's words and the market's actions have diverged in ways that matter for steepness.
body:
## Introduction

As a former central-bank economist, I have learned to be wary of reading too much into any single week of market moves. But the recent behaviour of the Japanese government bond curve deserves more than a passing glance. The Bank of Japan has been carefully signalling its intentions, and yet the long end of the curve has responded in ways that suggest investors are pricing something else entirely. In this newsletter, I want to separate what the BoJ actually said from what the market did, and then consider what that means for the steepness between the 10-year and 30-year sectors.

Let me start with the facts as I see them. The BoJ's policy statement and the Governor's press conference were, as usual, meticulously hedged. The bank reiterated its commitment to achieving the 2 percent inflation target in a sustainable manner, and it noted that it would not hesitate to take additional easing measures if necessary. That is standard language. What was less standard was the slight adjustment to the yield curve control framework, which now allows the 10-year yield to fluctuate in a range of plus or minus 0.5 percent, rather than the previous 0.25 percent. This was not a tightening per se, but it was a widening of the tolerance band. The market, however, treated it as a signal that the bank was preparing to exit its ultra-loose policy sooner than expected.

## What the BoJ said versus what the market heard

The distinction here is crucial. The BoJ explicitly said that the change was intended to improve the functioning of the bond market, not to signal a change in the monetary policy stance. Governor Kuroda, in his remarks, emphasised that the bank would continue with quantitative and qualitative easing with yield curve control as long as necessary to maintain the momentum toward the price stability target. He also said that the bank would closely monitor the impact of the wider band on market functioning and would adjust as needed. In other words, the bank was trying to buy itself more flexibility without committing to a tightening cycle.

The market, however, heard something different. Within minutes of the announcement, the 10-year JGB yield jumped to the top of the new band, and the 30-year yield rose even more sharply. By the end of the week, the 10-year yield had settled around 0.45 percent, while the 30-year yield had climbed to about 1.45 percent. That represents a steepening of roughly 100 basis points between the two tenors, compared with a spread of about 80 basis points a month earlier. The move was not uniform across the curve; the belly of the curve, particularly the 7-year and 10-year sectors, saw the most pronounced selling, while the very short end remained anchored near zero.

Why did the long end react so violently? Part of it is mechanical. The wider band effectively removed a cap on the 10-year yield, and investors extrapolated that to mean that the bank would eventually allow longer yields to rise as well. But there is also a fundamental story. Japanese inflation has been running above the BoJ's target for several months, albeit largely due to cost-push factors such as energy and food prices. The bank has argued that these are transitory, but the market is not so sure. If inflation becomes more persistent, the bank may be forced to tighten, and that would put upward pressure on the entire curve, but especially on the long end where duration risk is highest.

## The role of foreign investors

Another factor that I think is often overlooked is the behaviour of foreign investors. In recent years, Japanese yields have been so low that many overseas funds have avoided the JGB market altogether. But with the wider band, the 10-year yield is now approaching levels that are more attractive on a hedged basis, especially for European investors who are used to negative rates. At the same time, the 30-year yield is high enough to draw in real-money buyers such as pension funds and insurers. This creates a two-way flow that can amplify steepness. When the 10-year yield rises, foreign investors may buy, which caps the rise at the short end. But when the 30-year yield rises, domestic life insurers may step in, but they are also mindful of their duration gaps and may not be as aggressive. The net effect is that the long end can move more freely.

I should also mention the role of the US Treasury market. The correlation between JGB and US Treasury yields has been strong, particularly at the long end. When US 30-year yields rise, Japanese 30-year yields tend to follow, even if the BoJ is not tightening. This is partly due to arbitrage and partly due to sentiment. So the recent steepening in the JGB curve is not solely a Japanese story; it is also a reflection of global yield dynamics.

## Implications for curve steepness

So where does that leave us? The 10-year versus 30-year spread is now wider than it has been at any point in the past five years. In my view, this steepness is likely to persist for a while, but I would be cautious about extrapolating too far. The BoJ has shown that it is willing to intervene in the market to keep yields from rising too quickly. It has already announced unscheduled bond-buying operations to cap the 10-year yield at the top of its band. If the 30-year yield rises too far, the bank might also extend its operations to longer maturities, although it has been reluctant to do so because it wants to avoid the appearance of monetising government debt.

Moreover, the economic fundamentals do not yet support a sustained steepening. Japan's growth is still fragile, and the output gap is negative. Wage growth, while picking up, remains modest. The BoJ's own forecasts show inflation falling back below 2 percent in the next fiscal year. If that happens, the market may have to reprice its expectations, and the long end could rally, flattening the curve. But if inflation proves stickier, or if the global economy strengthens, then the steepening could continue.

## Conclusion

In conclusion, the recent steepening of the JGB curve between the 10-year and 30-year sectors is a classic case of the market interpreting a technical adjustment as a policy shift. The BoJ has tried to be clear that it is not tightening, but the market is not convinced. As an ex-central-bank economist, I am inclined to take the bank at its word, but I also recognise that markets often move ahead of policy. The key will be whether the BoJ can maintain its yield curve control without allowing the long end to drift too far. If it cannot, then we may see further steepening, and that would have implications for global bond markets as well. For now, I would watch the 30-year yield closely, and be prepared for volatility. This is a market that is still finding its footing in a new regime.
